name: Methane Processing Bioreactor
description: Introduces methanotrophic bacterial symbionts into a modified section of the upper digestive tract, allowing the user to process methane gas as a supplementary energy source. In Meridian 88's industrial underbelly, methane leaks from decomposing waste, aging infrastructure, and industrial processes are constant. The modification allows the user to breathe in methane-contaminated air without toxicity and extract caloric energy from the gas. It also functions as personal safety equipment — a Methanotroph Mod user can work in methane-rich environments that would asphyxiate or poison an unmodified human. Gravemoss Biofoundry developed it for waste processing workers and sewer maintenance crews. The modification has a distinctive tell — users exhale carbon dioxide and water vapor with a faintly sweet, organic smell.
source_organism: Methylococcus capsulatus (methanotrophic bacterium), synthetic respiratory-tract integration scaffold
procedure: Oral retroviral treatment establishing methanotrophic colony in modified pharyngeal tissue, single dose
side_effects: Sweet-smelling breath that some find pleasant and others find unsettling
Mild euphoria in methane-rich environments (the modification processes the gas but doesn't prevent all neurological effects)
Bacterial colony requires regular methane exposure to remain viable — urban environments usually provide enough
Rare: colony overgrowth causing chronic nausea
social_perception: Working-class modification associated with waste processing, sewer work, and industrial maintenance. Carries the social status of a hard hat. Some users develop a preference for methane-rich environments, spending off-hours in industrial zones — a habit that reads as eccentric at best.
story_hooks: A Methanotroph Mod user detects a methane concentration in a residential building that indicates a massive leak beneath the foundation — the building is sitting on a decomposition pocket that could explode

A waste worker's methanotrophic colony begins processing other gases — including airborne pharmaceutical compounds — turning the user into an inadvertent drug metabolizer who gets high from walking past certain factories
